rich_summary: This section (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter III) addresses Arjuna’s confusion about whether knowledge and devotion are superior to action. Krishna explains that there are two spiritual paths—knowledge and disciplined action—but no one can truly avoid action. Instead, one should perform one’s duty without attachment to results. Actions offered as sacrifice sustain the cosmic order, linking humans, gods, and nature in a reciprocal cycle. Great leaders must act responsibly because others imitate them. The wise act without ego, understanding that nature’s qualities perform all works. Krishna identifies desire and anger as the great enemies that cloud knowledge. The teaching culminates in the principle of svadharma: performing one’s own duty, even imperfectly, is better than doing another’s well.

highlight_spans.why: Defines the peaceful state attained by renouncing desire and ego, establishing the spiritual ideal preceding the chapter’s discussion of action.
Arjuna’s heartfelt confusion about why he is urged into battle despite praise of devotion and knowledge.
Krishna’s core teaching that no one can remain inactive and that disciplined action is superior to inaction.
Explains the cosmic 'wheel' of sacrifice linking work, nature, the gods, and the Vedas—central to the Gita’s philosophy of duty.
The famous doctrine that one’s own duty, even imperfectly performed, is better than perfectly performing another’s.
Krishna identifies desire and wrath as the destructive inner enemies that obscure knowledge.

top_scenes.scene_text: Krishna standing beside Arjuna’s chariot on the battlefield, calmly teaching while armies wait in tense silence.
A symbolic cosmic wheel turning—humans offering sacrifice, gods sending rain, crops growing, and beings nourished in a continuous cycle.
A figure whose clear inner light of knowledge is gradually covered by smoky flames representing desire and anger.
